entries.modern_form: PIE *dʰéǵʰōm 'earth' (Pokorny's ĝhðem-, ĝhðom-, gen.-abl. ĝh(d)m-es; Watkins/AHD dhghem-)
entries.note: The root itself is real and correctly labelled and glossed: Pokorny IEW 414-416 heads the entry 'ghdem-, ghdom-, Gen.-ablative gh(d)m-es' with the meaning 'earth, man, dragon', and Nourai's first spelling 'Ghdhem' is simply his own rendering of Pokorny's ĝhðem- (he writes the interdental ð as dh). The gloss 'earth' and the language label 'Indo-European' are right, and every branch drawn on the page (Av./OP zam-, Latin humus/homo/humanus, Greek khthon, Germanic *gumon-) is in Pokorny's and Watkins' own material. The flag is only for the SECOND form in the box. The printed page (pdf p.180, image kept at data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/180.png) really does read 'Ghdhem, Dhehem', so the extraction is faithful; but 'Dhehem' is an impossible reconstruction — no source knows it. It is Nourai's misprint for Watkins/AHD's metathesised variant 'dhghem- (*dheghom)' (AHD Appendix, quoted verbatim under 'A word for the earth can be reconstructed as dhghem- (*dheghom)'), i.e. it should read 'Dhghem' or 'Dheghom'. Note also that the two forms are not two roots but the two conventional orderings of the same cluster (ĝhð- vs dhgh-), which Pokorny explains as a metathesis of *g(e)dhom-, *gh(e)dhom-. Two substantive weak spots further down the chart: node 4's gloss (Khwarazm as a 'city' and as the Airyanem Vaejo) and node 15, which the book labels Greek although its own source AHD says Germanic.
entries.note_fa: جعبهٔ ریشه در بنیاد درست است: پوکورنی در «فرهنگ ریشه‌شناختی هندواروپایی» صفحهٔ ۴۱۴ تا ۴۱۶ سرواژهٔ «ghdem-, ghdom-» را با معنای «زمین، آدمی، اژدها» آورده است و صورت نخستِ نورایی یعنی Ghdhem همان ĝhðem- پوکورنی است (او دندانی‌میان‌دندانیِ ð را dh می‌نویسد). برچسبِ زبان (هندواروپایی) و معنای «زمین» نیز درست است و همهٔ شاخه‌های نمودار — zam- اوستایی و پارسی باستان، humus و homo لاتینی، khthōn یونانی و *gumōn- ژرمنی — در مادهٔ خودِ پوکورنی و واتکینز هست. اما صورت دومِ جعبه، یعنی «Dhehem»، در هیچ مأخذی نیست و صورتی ناممکن است؛ تصویر صفحهٔ چاپی نشان می‌دهد که خطای خوانشِ اسکن نیست بلکه خطای چاپی خودِ کتاب است و باید «Dhghem» (یا Dheghom) می‌بود، یعنی صورتِ قلب‌شدهٔ همان ریشه که فرهنگ American Heritage به کار می‌برد. این دو، دو ریشهٔ جدا نیستند بلکه دو ترتیبِ متعارفِ همان خوشهٔ همخوانی‌اند و پوکورنی خود آن را قلب (metathesis) از *g(e)dhom- می‌داند.

nodes.derivation: Proto-Iranian *dzam- (< PIE *dʰéǵʰōm, with the regular Indo-Iranian palatalisation and the Iranian *ǰʰ > z) is directly attested as Avestan zam- f. 'earth': Bartholomae, Altiranisches Wörterbuch cols. 1662-1664, gives the paradigm 'zam- f. "Erde"; zam (AS.) ... zəmō (GS.) ... zəmi (LS.)' with the two chief senses 'earth as opposed to sky' and 'earth/land as opposed to water'. Sanskrit kṣam- (gen. jmaḥ) and Greek khthōn are the exact cognates. In Old Persian the free word for 'earth' is būmi- (usually written with the ideogram BU); zam- survives only as a bound second member, precisely in the two compounds Nourai draws below it — uzma- < *ud-zma- and Uvārazmi- — so the double label 'Avestan / Old Persian' is defensible for the stem but the OP is compound-only. Nourai's gloss 'earth' is exact.
nodes.derivation_fa: ستاکِ ایرانیِ باستانِ *dzam- (از هندواروپاییِ آغازینِ *dʰéǵʰōm، با کامی‌شدنِ هندوایرانی و سپس تبدیلِ *ǰʰ به z در ایرانی) در اوستا به‌صورتِ zam- (مؤنث) «زمین» به‌جا مانده است؛ بارتولومه در ستون‌های ۱۶۶۲ تا ۱۶۶۴ صورت‌های صرفیِ zam (رایی)، zəmō (اضافی) و zəmi (دری) را با دو معنای اصلی «زمین در برابر آسمان» و «خشکی در برابر آب» می‌آورد. هم‌ریشه‌های دقیقِ آن سنسکریت kṣam- (اضافی jmaḥ) و یونانی khthōn است. در پارسیِ باستان واژهٔ آزادِ «زمین» būmi- است و zam- تنها در ترکیب می‌آید، همان دو ترکیبی که نورایی زیرِ همین گره کشیده است: uzma- و Uvārazmi-. پس معنا و برچسبِ گره درست است، جز آنکه صورتِ پارسیِ باستان تنها در ترکیب گواهی شده است.

nodes.derivation: New Persian زمین continues Middle Persian zamīg [zmyk'] 'earth' (MacKenzie, Concise Pahlavi Dictionary p.96: 'zamīg [z-, zmyk' | M zmyg, N zamī] earth'; Manichaean MP zmyg), itself from Proto-Iranian *dzam- + the MP -īg suffix. Regular MP → NP loss of final -g gives زمی zamī, still the normal word in Ferdowsi and in Horn's citations (Šāhnāma I.134, I.178 v.877); the current form زمین is that stem enlarged by the adjectival/nominal suffix -īn, exactly as Mo'in states in his footnote to Borhan-e Qate' ('و زمین از همین زم است ... با پسوند ین'), and it had already displaced zamī by the classical period. Nyberg calls zamī 'archaic form for modern zamīn'. The gloss 'earth' is right; the node's only omission is that the immediate ancestor is the Middle Persian form, not Avestan zam- directly.
nodes.derivation_fa: «زمین» دنبالهٔ فارسیِ میانهٔ zamīg (نوشتهٔ zmyk'، در متونِ مانوی zmyg) است — مکنزی در «فرهنگ کوچکِ پهلوی» ص ۹۶ می‌آورد: «zamīg ... زمین» — و آن خود از ایرانیِ باستانِ *dzam- با پسوندِ -īg ساخته شده است. بنا بر قاعدهٔ آواییِ گذر از فارسیِ میانه به فارسیِ نو، گافِ پایانی می‌افتد و «زمی» به دست می‌آید که هنوز در شاهنامه به کار می‌رود (هرن، شمارهٔ ۶۶۷، با شاهدِ شاهنامه)؛ صورتِ امروزیِ «زمین» همان ستاک با پسوندِ «ـین» است، چنان‌که معین در حاشیهٔ برهان قاطع می‌نویسد: «و زمین از همین زم است ... با پسوندِ ین». نیبرگ نیز «زمی» را صورتِ کهنِ «زمین» می‌خواند. پس ادعای نورایی درست است؛ تنها نکته آنکه واسطهٔ فارسیِ میانه در نمودار نیامده است.

nodes.derivation: This is Kent's analysis reproduced letter for letter. Kent, Old Persian, Lexicon s.v.: 'Uvārazmi- sb. "Chorasmia", a province of the Persian Empire: Elam. ma-ra-iš-mi-iš, Akk. hu-ma-ri-iz-ma-\', Gk. Khōrasmiē, Av. asf. x'āirizəm. From u- "good" + vāra- "?" (§126, §148.III), + zmi- (§95, §120, §152) to zam- "land".' Nourai's segmentation u-vāra-zmi, his gloss 'good ... land' with the ellipsis, and even his NOTE 'the meaning of "vāra" is not clear' are Kent's question mark rendered into words — so as a report of the cited source the node is exact. It is marked plausible rather than confirmed because Kent's is only one of several current analyses of the name and not the favoured one: the first element is more usually taken as *hwar-/xwar- either 'sun' (Bosworth: 'the land from which the sun rises') or *xwār- 'low' ('the lowland', Khwarazm being the lowest part of Central Asia), and Yaqut already offered a folk etymology xwār 'food' + razm. What is not in doubt is the second element -zmi- < zam- 'earth, land', which is the only part the arrow from the root actually needs. One label correction: Uvārazmi- is Old Persian (DB 1.16, DPe, DNa, DSe, DSm, XPh); the Avestan counterpart is a different form, x'āirizəm.
nodes.derivation_fa: این گره واژه‌به‌واژه تحلیلِ کنت است. کنت در واژه‌نامهٔ «پارسی باستان» ذیلِ Uvārazmi- «خوارزم، ساتراپی‌ای از شاهنشاهی هخامنشی» می‌نویسد: «از u- (خوب) + vāra- (؟) + zmi- که به zam- «زمین» بازمی‌گردد»، و صورت‌های ایلامی، اکدی، یونانی (Khōrasmiē) و اوستایی (x'āirizəm) را نیز می‌آورد. بخش‌بندیِ نورایی، معنای «سرزمینِ خوب…» با نقطه‌چین، و حتی یادداشتِ «معنای vāra روشن نیست» همان علامتِ پرسشِ کنت است که به جمله درآمده؛ پس گره در گزارشِ مأخذ کاملاً امین است. اما «با احتیاط پذیرفتنی» است، زیرا تحلیلِ کنت تنها یکی از تحلیل‌های موجود است و امروز رایج‌تر آن است که جزءِ نخست را *xwar- «خورشید» (بازورث: «سرزمینی که خورشید از آن برمی‌آید») یا *xwār- «پست، فرود» («سرزمینِ پست») بگیرند؛ یاقوت نیز ریشه‌شناسیِ عامیانهٔ «خوار (خوراک) + رزم» را آورده است. آنچه مورد اختلاف نیست جزءِ دومِ -zmi- از zam- «زمین» است و همین برای درستیِ پیکانِ نمودار بس است. یک نکتهٔ برچسبی: Uvārazmi- پارسیِ باستان است نه اوستایی؛ برابرِ اوستایی‌اش x'āirizəm است.

Quote: 'From u- "good" + vāra- "?" ... + zmi- ... to zam- "land".' The '?' is exactly Nourai's NOTE.

consulted.note: The Avestan Chorasmia name could not be located in the OCR of the Altiranisches Wörterbuch (the diacritic-heavy x'āirizəm defeats the scan); the AiW is however the source Kent quotes for the Avestan accusative form.

'The only survival of separate declensional forms is nom. Uvarazmiy, with original -ī, replaced in later inscriptions by Uvārazmiš' — the name is solidly Old Persian and inscriptionally attested, e.g. DSe 22 'Suguda : Uvarazmiš'.

Lists Bosworth's *xwar 'sun' + *zam 'land' ('the land from which the sun rises'), the 'lowland' analysis (*xwār 'low' + zam), and Yaqut's xwār 'food' + razm — i.e. the second element zam- is common ground, the first is disputed and Kent's u- 'good' is not the modern favourite.

nodes.derivation: The three forms are real and are Kent's: 'huvârazmîš' is the Old Persian nominative Uvārazmiš (DNa 23, DSe 22, DSm 9, XPh 21f; the earlier nominative Uvārazmiy stands at DB 1.16 and DPe 16f), Nourai writing the initial u- as hu- because he takes it as the prefix hu- 'good'; 'xvarazmîš' is the same name with the later Iranian xʷ- development that yields MP/NP Xwārazm; 'xvârizem' is Kent's Avestan accusative x'āirizəm. The forms are therefore sound. What is not sound is the gloss. (a) Uvārazmiš in the inscriptions is a dahyu-, a province/country in the satrapy lists (Bactria, Sogdia, Chorasmia, Drangiana...), not 'an ancient city'. (b) The identification with Airyanəm Vaēǰah, the Avestan homeland of Vd. 1.1, is a nineteenth/twentieth-century hypothesis (Markwart; in Persian scholarship Dehkhoda, who calls Khwarazm 'the cradle of the Aryan tribe'; Elton Daniel still calls it 'the most likely locale'), and it is contested — Witzel places Airyanəm Vaēǰah in the Afghan highlands. (c) 'Now it is known as Khiva' repeats Klein's and Lokotsch's nineteenth-century shorthand, in which the whole region was named after the Khanate of Khiva; the historical Khwarazm oasis is much larger than the town of Khiva, and its old capitals were Kāth and Gurgānj (Urgench).

nodes.derivation: Two of the three are straightforward. خوارزم is the regular New Persian continuant of Old Persian Uvārazmiš / Middle Persian Xwārazm: OP initial u- of the compound, once it was no longer felt as hu- 'good', was refashioned as the labialised xʷ- that Persian writes خو-, and the -iš nominative ending was lost with the collapse of OP nominal inflection; the modern spelling خوارزم has the silent wāw of xʷ- (as in خواهر, خواندن). خوارزمی is the Persian nisba in -ī 'of Khwarazm', used both of the language (Mo'in's footnote 6 in Borhan sends the reader to p.22 of his Introduction 'on the language of Khwarazm') and as the surname of Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad b. Mūsā, whose Kitāb al-jabr wa'l-muqābala is correctly described in the node's NOTE. The third word is the weak link: خیوه / خیوق (Khiva, Khīvaq) is a distinct toponym of unknown origin — one theory does take it from Khwārazm through a Turkic intermediate Khīvarezem, and the local legend derives it from the well Kheyvak dug by Shem — and Borhan itself keeps them apart, treating خیوق as a place within the Khwarazm territory ('خیوق: نام ولایتی ... اولکای خوارزم') with a cross-reference 'خیوه: رك: خیوق'. Drawing خیوه as simply equal to خوارزم repeats Klein's and Lokotsch's nineteenth-century shorthand (Khwarazm = the khanate of Khiva) rather than an etymological derivation, hence plausible, not confirmed. The Hāfez line quoted in the box ('دانی کجاست جای تو خوارزم یا خجند') is genuine and merely illustrates the name.

nodes.derivation: الخوارزمي is the ordinary Arabic nisba: the Persian toponym خوارزم with the Arabic relative-adjective suffix -ī and the article al-, 'the man from Khwarazm'. It is the by-name of Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Mūsā (fl. c.820), an astronomer and mathematician of the Bayt al-Ḥikma in Baghdad under al-Maʾmūn, whose Kitāb al-jabr wa'l-muqābala gave Europe the word algebra and whose arithmetic (surviving only in the Latin Liber Algorismi de numero Indorum) gave it the decimal place-value system and, from his name, algorism. The node is a personal name, not a common noun, so the 'Arabic' label means only that the nisba is formed by Arabic morphology on a Persian base — the derivation from node 5 is exact.

nodes.derivation: Medieval Latin algorismus arose in the twelfth-century Toledo translation movement: the Latin version of al-Khwārizmī's lost arithmetic circulates as Liber Algorismi de numero Indorum / Dixit Algorizmi, where the author's nisba is transliterated as the book's name and then taken as the name of the method. Klein calls it 'the inexact transliteration of Arab. al-Khowarizmi'; the -ismus ending was helped along by the familiar Latin/Greek noun suffix, and the variant algorithmus appears beside it under the pull of Greek arithmos 'number' (Lokotsch 890 states this explicitly: 'daher wurde lat. algorithmus, algorismus [mit Anlehnung an gr. ἀριθμός] die Bezeichnung für das Rechnen mit ar. Ziffern'). The gloss 'the Arabic system of numerals' is Klein's own wording.

nodes.derivation: A twentieth-century European loan back into Persian, and thus the closing of a full circle: a Khwarazmian toponym → an Arabic nisba → Medieval Latin → French → modern Persian. The donor is French algorithme (Persian technical vocabulary of the Reza Shah and post-war period came overwhelmingly through French), which explains the final -tm cluster of آلگوریتم rather than an English -thm pronounced /ðəm/. Nourai's spelling with alef-madda, آلگوریتم, renders the French [al-] with a long ā; the spelling now standard in Persian mathematics and computing is الگوریتم (and the Academy's Persian equivalent is خوارزمی or خوارزمیک — a deliberate restoration of the original name). The gloss 'a type of computational procedure' is right for the modern sense. Verdict confirmed for the fact and route of the borrowing; the only unverifiable point is Nourai's source, Moshiri's Farhang-e vazheha-ye Orupayi dar Farsi p.17, of which no copy could be found.

nodes.derivation: Middle English algorisme appears early in the thirteenth century, borrowed from Old French algorisme and denoting reckoning with the nine Arabic figures and the zero (as against reckoning on the abacus, 'augrim' in Chaucer). Modern algorithm is a separate, later entry, 1690s, from the refashioned French algorithme, and only in the mid twentieth century did it settle on its present sense 'a finite, effective computational procedure' under the influence of computing and of Church-Turing style definitions. Both English words therefore descend from the French node exactly as drawn; Klein sets them out in one line and Lokotsch's list ends 'engl. algorism, algorithm "Rechenart"'.

nodes.derivation: Kent's lexicon has exactly this: 'uzma- adj. as sb. "that which is up from the earth, stake": from ud- "up" + zma- to zam- "earth"', with the phonology stated at §84-85 — the prefix ud 'up' (Av. us-/uz-, Skt. ud, PIE *ud) assimilates its d completely before the following z, giving uz-, and the resulting long cluster is shortened. The word is attested only in the locative compound uzmayā-patiy, in Darius' formula for impaling rebels: DB 2.76 'pasāva-šim Hagmatānaiy uzmayāpatiy akunavam' — 'afterwards I put him on the stake at Ecbatana' (also DB 2.91, 3.52, 3.92). Nourai's gloss 'grown up from ground' is Kent's 'that which is up from the earth' with the actual referent — the impaling stake — silently dropped, which makes the box read as though it were a word for a plant. The verdict is plausible rather than confirmed because the etymology is not unanimous: Hübschmann, Persische Studien no. 667, expressly rejects it ('Ap. uzmayā-patiy kar "kreuzigen (Bang: pfählen)" gehört schwerlich hierher'), against Horn who had put it under zamīn, and Kent himself flags dissent ('otherwise Wackernagel KZ 61.208; Lommel OLZ 37.180 n.2; König RuID 72'). Kent's *ud-zma- is nevertheless the standard analysis today.

nodes.derivation: All three are the standard Latin reflexes of this root and all three stand in Nourai's cited source. humus f. 'ground, soil' is the suffixed o-grade *(dʰ)ǵʰom-o-, a thematised remake of an older consonant stem *ǵʰom-, which kept the feminine gender of the old *dʰéǵʰōm (Ernout-Meillet: 'comme les autres noms de la terre, tellūs, terra, par réaction du genre sur la forme'); the locative humī 'on the ground' preserves the old case form, and humilis 'low' (: Gk. khthamalós) is built on it. homō, -inis 'human being' is the suffixed o-grade *(dʰ)ǵʰom-on- 'earthling', with Old Latin hemō still visible in the accusative hemōnem and in nemō 'nobody' < *ne-hemō; the Oscan-Umbrian cognates humuns / homonus show the same stem. hūmānus 'human, humane' belongs here too, though with an unexplained long ū (Walde-Pokorny: 'mit unklarem Vokalismus'); Watkins guards it with '(in part)'. Nourai's gloss 'kind' for humanus is copied straight from Watkins' 'Latin hūmānus, human, kind, humane'. The one thing the box does not show is that homo/hūmānus and humus are two different derivatives of the root rather than a chain.

nodes.derivation: Each of the five English words takes the Latin route drawn in the box, and all five appear in the AHD entry that the parent node cites. humble is ME humble/umble from Old French humble, from Latin humilem, acc. of humilis 'low, lit. on the ground', a derivative of humus (Klein s.v. humble: 'fr. L. humilem ... lit. "on the ground", fr. humus'); humility is Old French humilite from Latin humilitātem. human comes through Old French humain from Latin hūmānus, and humane is the same word: the two were a single English word into the seventeenth century, and only then did spelling and stress split them into 'of mankind' and 'kindly' — hence Watkins' bracketing '(HUMANE)'. homicide is Old French homicide from Latin homicīdium 'manslaughter' and homicīda 'man-slayer', i.e. homo + -cīda (caedere 'to cut, kill'), and so belongs to the homo branch, not the humus branch. The box's grouping in three lines in fact tracks that distinction correctly: humble/humility from humus, human/humane from hūmānus, homicide from homo.

nodes.derivation: The word is real but the language is wrong, and Nourai's own cited source says so. AHD (Watkins) reads: 'dhghem-. Earth. 1. Suffixed zero-grade form *(dh)ghm-on-, "earthling," in GERMANIC *gumon- in Old English guma, man: BRIDEGROOM.' Nourai has copied the reconstruction *gumon- but labelled the box Greek. There is no Greek word gumon and none could be: PIE *dʰǵʰ- gives Greek khth-, so this root's Greek reflexes are khthṓn 'earth', khamaí 'on the ground', khthamalós 'low' — all with initial khth-/kh-, and all listed a line above in the same AHD entry. The form *gumōn- is Proto-Germanic, whence Gothic guma, Old Norse gumi, Old English guma, Old High German gomo 'man', and the compound *brūdi-gumô that gives German Bräutigam and, via node 16, English bridegroom. Walde-Pokorny I 663 and Mann both put guma in Germanic; Klein s.v. bridegroom writes 'OE. guma, "man", which is rel. to OS. gumo, ON. gumi, OFris. goma, OHG. gomo, Goth. guma, "man", and cogn. with L. homo'. The printed page (image at data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/180.png) really does read 'Greek', so the extraction is faithful and the mislabelling is the book's own; the label should be Germanic (or Old English guma).

nodes.derivation: The English word does descend from *gumōn-, so the arrow's substance is right even though its parent box is mislabelled (node 15). Old English brȳdguma = brȳd 'bride' + guma 'man', i.e. 'the bride's man', matching Old Saxon brūdigomo, Old Norse brúðgumi, Old High German brūtigomo, German Bräutigam (Gothic went its own way with brūþsfaþs 'bride's lord'). In Middle English the word is still brudgume, bridegome; guma then died out of the language, and in the sixteenth century the now-meaningless second element was replaced by folk etymology with the familiar groom 'lad, serving-man' — the sole source of the -r-, which has no etymological standing. The word is thus, through guma < Germanic *gumōn- < PIE *(dʰ)ǵʰm-on- 'earthling', a cousin of Latin homo and, through the root, of Persian zamīn: the bridegroom is literally 'the bride's earthling'.
nodes.derivation_fa: واژهٔ انگلیسی به‌راستی از *gumōn- می‌آید، پس مضمونِ پیکان درست است هرچند جعبهٔ بالادستش (گرهٔ ۱۵) برچسبِ نادرست دارد. در انگلیسیِ کهن brȳdguma است، یعنی brȳd «عروس» + guma «مرد»، «مردِ عروس»، برابر با brūdigomo ساکسونِ کهن، brúðgumi نورسِ کهن، brūtigomo آلمانیِ علیای کهن و Bräutigam آلمانی (گوتی راهِ دیگری رفته و brūþsfaþs «خداوندِ عروس» دارد). در انگلیسیِ میانه هنوز brudgume و bridegome است؛ سپس واژهٔ guma از زبان افتاد و در سدهٔ شانزدهم جزءِ دومِ بی‌معنا شده را به ریشه‌شناسیِ عامیانه با groom «پسر، نوکر» جانشین کردند — و «ر» این واژه یکسره از همین‌جاست و هیچ پشتوانهٔ ریشه‌شناختی ندارد. بدین‌سان bridegroom از راهِ guma و ژرمنیِ *gumōn- و هندواروپاییِ *(dʰ)ǵʰm-on- «زمینی» پسرعمویِ homo لاتینی و، از راهِ ریشه، هم‌ریشهٔ «زمین» فارسی است: داماد به‌لفظ «خاکیِ عروس» است.
